name: Sam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy, in a good way. I'm doing software engineering, and I live in a five-person house share above a laundrette, which smells amazing and costs less than anywhere else I found. I have lectures four days a week, and I spend a lot of evenings building things, like a little bot that posts the bin collection days into our house chat. On Tuesday and Thursday I tutor two teenagers in maths over video call, which pays my bills, roughly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about tutoring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Watching a kid go from 'I hate this' to 'oh, that's all it is'. I use an AI assistant to plan lessons and generate practice questions, then I fix the mistakes it makes before the kids see them. It's quicker than writing everything myself, and the kids like when I show them how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, and I'd laugh a bit, because I use these tools daily and I know where they fall over. I'd tell friends it's a good assistant and a bad boss. I'd probably post that the loudest predictions are by people who sell the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay, because I already work with the tools and my skills would still be wanted. The worry isn't AI, it's money. My loan covers fees, but I live on what I earn, and if two students drop their lessons, my month is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep tutoring and add a third student, and I'd keep building small projects for a portfolio. I'd start putting ten pounds a week into a savings pot, because I've never had one. And I'd apply to a summer internship at a small software firm instead of waiting for the big names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually, with a thin layer of nerves. A normal world is one where my skills keep their value, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the nerves be about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and the unpredictable income. If one of my students stops, I lose a third of my income overnight, and AI has nothing to do with that. That's the thing that wakes me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your tutoring prep is AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About half, I'd guess. I generate questions and check the answers myself, and I add a joke or a real-life example so it doesn't feel like a worksheet from a machine.

I'd post that the loudest predictions come from people selling the **tools**.
think: I'm okay about my skills, because I already work with the **tools** daily.
The real worry is **income**: two lost students would wreck my month.
do: Keep tutoring and add a **third** student.
Put ten pounds a week into a first **savings** pot.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a small software firm.
feel: Pretty **good**, with a thin layer of nerves about rent.

steps.text: Add a third tutoring student before the autumn exams
Put ten pounds a week into a savings pot
Apply for a summer internship at a small software firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and rough in equal parts. I'd tell friends that the people who learn to work with AI get a head start, and the people who ignore it get squeezed. I'd also say employers should be honest about which jobs are changing, because the quiet cuts are the worst ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good position but not a safe one. I'm good with the tools, but so will be every other graduate by then, so being good with them isn't a special edge. Junior coding jobs shrink first, and I'd need something that sets me apart, like a niche or a few real projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on one niche, maybe accessibility tools or education software, since I know tutoring. I'd build a small app for tutors and try to get a handful of real users, then put it on my CV. I'd also take on more tutoring in the meantime because that's actual income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. I'm aware that sounds smug when other people are scared. But I'd also feel a slight pressure, because everyone else will be racing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your edge real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having shipped something that people use. When anyone can generate code, the person who has real users and knows what they actually want is the one who gets hired. Tutoring helps me, because I know the problem from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your house share would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani, who studies translation. If AI takes over most translation, the course feels very exposed. I'd tell Dani to learn the tools fast and to find a specialism, like medical or legal translation, where mistakes matter.

I'd tell friends employers should be honest about which jobs are **changing**.

fieldNote: He knows AI skill is not a **differentiator** once everyone has it.

steps.text: Build a small scheduling app for tutors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, scarily fast, and that we're not ready. I'd tell friends to stop assuming the old plan works and to ask what they'd want to do anyway. Online I'd say that governments should do something, like a safety net, and quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my plan breaks. The degree isn't finished for another three years, and entry-level coding would be one of the first things to go. I'd be in a world where the thing I trained for is done by AI cheaper than me, and where nobody has a plan for the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn the tutoring into something bigger straight away, maybe a small tutoring service, because teaching and human trust might hold longer. I'd also start looking at hands-on options like robotics maintenance, since robots come about three years later and someone has to service them. And I'd cut every spend that isn't food, rent and data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thrilled and terrified, which is a strange mix. Part of me wants to see it, and part of me is staring at the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your tutoring students' parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not going anywhere and that the human part of teaching still matters. If AI can teach everything, people will still want somebody who knows their name and shows up. I'd lean on that as my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter that robots lag by three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It means that if I can get into maintenance or installation I'd have time to build a living. But it's a gamble, because I'd be guessing which jobs last.

say: I'd say it's **scarily fast** and we're not ready.
I'd say governments should build a **safety net** quickly.
think: My plan **breaks**: entry-level coding goes first, long before I graduate.
The world has no plan for the **rest of us**.
do: Turn my tutoring into a small **service** straight away.

Cut every spend that isn't food, rent and **data**.
feel: **Thrilled** and terrified, curious but staring at the loan.
S2.quote: If AI can teach everything, people will still want somebody who knows their name and shows up

steps.text: Turn the tutoring into a small paid tutoring service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something, so people should act now. I'd tell friends to learn how these systems work, not just how to ask them questions. Online I'd probably share what I'm building and ask for feedback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I have one real shot. I'd be 23 when it lands, probably in my first job or just leaving university, which is fine if I'm already doing something that matters. If I only have the degree, it's weaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish year one with a decent project, apply for a placement, and aim at companies that build AI tools rather than ones being replaced by them. I'd take AI safety and ethics modules if the course offers any. I'd also keep the tutoring going and build up a small cushion, maybe a month of rent, over the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and keen. I like deadlines, and this one is big enough to focus me. I'd probably feel more nervous in the third and fourth years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you had only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the plan to finish a long degree and go for whatever lets me earn fastest. With five years I can choose a plan, but with two I'd be grabbing anything that pays rent. That's the real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want other first-years to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk about it. Most of my course doesn't discuss it because it feels uncool to worry. I'd start a little group to share what we're building and who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and it's the one scenario where I'd argue we can shape it. I'd tell friends to push for rules and retraining now. I'd say it's a chance to design the transition instead of reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel pretty calm. By 28 I could have a company or a good career, and the money to take a risk. The ones I worry about are people with fewer options, like Dani with translation, or my mum, who works in a pharmacy and might see her job change a few years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a placement, try a start-up with friends, and keep a cushion. I'd stay current by using new tools the week they come out. And I'd spend some of my time on a project that helps tutors or schools, because that's something I'd want to exist anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a gap in it for the people who won't have my options. Ten years feels fair to me, and that's a privilege.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help her think about moving into the clinical side of pharmacy, where a person is needed. I'd spend my first savings on helping my mum retrain, before spending anything on myself. She's done everything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk of feeling this relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I stop pushing. A decade is long enough to coast and then get hit. So I'd set myself yearly checkpoints and stick to them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives me no time to build anything real before the ground moves. What would help is a safety net that kicks in quickly, plus access to the tools and training for people who can't afford them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm relaxed because I use the tools daily. I'm not relaxed, I'm just early, and being early is only an edge until everybody else catches up. That's why I keep building.

headlineQuote: I'm not relaxed, I'm just early, and being early is only an edge until everybody else catches up
portrait: Sam is an **18-year-old** software engineering first-year in a five-person house share above a laundrette.
He is progressive, curious and adaptive, using AI tools every day and tutoring two teenagers to pay his bills.
His real worry is **income**, since losing one student would cost him a third of his money.
He plans by building real products, taking placements and saving small amounts, and he worries about housemates and his mum.
His mood is mostly uneasy, rising to anxious at two years and calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, because he would have no time to build something real.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a fast **safety net** plus free training and tools for people who can't afford them.
